rationale: This qualitative study (based on 30 key-informant interviews alongside parliamentary and Auditor-General reports) examines how Zimbabwe's central government centralized municipal mandates—specifically transferring urban water and sanitation functions to the national parastatal ZINWA via a May 2005 ministerial directive before decentralizing them back in 2009, alongside centralizing vehicle licensing revenue in ZINARA. The dominant mechanism is institutional_structure_coordination (centralization vs. devolution, intergovernmental mandate and revenue allocation, and inter-municipal coordination/billing splits, with secondary discussion of bulk tariffs and bill cancellations under fees_tariffs_subsidies). Empirically, the paper evaluates co-equally central outcomes across effective_access (erratic water supply, severe rationing to two days per week, unpotable water, pipe bursts, deterioration of functional infrastructure, and reliance on unsafe wells) and administrative_outcome (collapse of municipal billing/revenue collection, staffing crises, intergovernmental sabotage, and municipal refusal to recognize ZINWA-approved connections across council boundaries), warranting primary_outcome_family = effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = multiple.
